title: The Fewest Stops to Refuel on the Way to the Goal

concept.title: Drive as far as you can; only when you are stuck, pretend you refuelled at the best station you passed
body: A car drives along a line from the position 0 to the position `target`, using 1 unit of fuel per unit of distance. It starts with `fuel` units. Along the way there are stations; at a station you may take **all** its fuel (the tank has no limit), but each time you stop is counted. What is the **fewest number of stops** needed to reach the target? Print -1 if it is impossible. For `target = 100`, `fuel = 10` and the stations `(10, 60) (20, 30) (30, 30) (60, 40)` the answer is 2: stop at the position 10 and then at 60.

The key observation is that the decision of **where** to stop can be postponed. Drive forward without stopping while the fuel lasts. All the stations passed on the way are candidates, and we may regret not having stopped at any of them. When the fuel is not enough to go on, we choose — *retroactively* — the passed station with the **most fuel** and count a stop there. This is optimal because stopping anywhere before the point of being stuck gives the same total reach afterwards: only the amount of fuel taken matters, so the biggest one is the best.

body.code:
heap = []                       # the fuel amounts of the stations passed (a max-heap)
reach = fuel                    # the farthest position we can reach with the stops made so far
i = stops = 0
while reach < target:
    while i < n and st[i][0] <= reach:     # the stations we can get to
        heappush(heap, -st[i][1]); i += 1
    if not heap:
        stops = -1; break                # stuck: nothing to refuel from
    reach += -heappop(heap)             # stop at the best passed station
    stops += 1
print(stops)

body: Each station enters the heap once and leaves it at most once, so the algorithm takes O(n log n). The variable `reach` is the total of the starting fuel and the fuel of all chosen stations. A dynamic programming solution `best[j] = the farthest position with j stops` needs O(n^2); the heap solution shows that the greedy choice "largest fuel among the reachable stations" is enough.

statement: A car starts at the position 0 with `fuel` units of fuel and must reach the position `target`; one unit of distance costs one unit of fuel. There are `n` stations at the given positions (increasing); at a station the car may stop and take all of its fuel (the tank is unlimited). Print the smallest number of stops needed to reach the target, or -1 if it cannot be reached.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, `target` and `fuel`: the number of stations, the distance to the goal and the fuel in the tank at the start.
Each of the next `n` lines has two numbers `d` and `f`: the position of a station and the fuel you can take there.
outputFormat: Print the smallest number of stops, or -1.
constraints: The stations are listed in increasing order of d, with 1 <= d < target.

examples.note: Stop at the positions 10 (60 fuel) and 60 (40 fuel): 2 stops.
The car cannot reach the station at 10 with 1 unit of fuel: -1.

hints: Drive while fuel lasts, collecting the fuel amounts of the stations passed.
When the fuel runs out, take the largest fuel among the stations passed.
Use a max-heap and count the stops.

explanation: The car drives as far as possible; the fuel amounts of the passed stations go into a max-heap, and whenever the target is not yet reachable the largest amount is taken (a stop is counted); if the heap is empty the goal cannot be reached.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

from heapq import heappush, heappop

n, target, fuel = map(int, input().split())
st = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

heap = []
reach = fuel
i = stops = 0
while reach < target:
    while i < n and st[i][0] <= reach:
        heappush(heap, -st[i][1])
        i += 1
    if not heap:
        stops = -1
        break
    reach -= heappop(heap)
    stops += 1
print(stops)
